# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–6 (Complete and Final – Updated 70)

## Setting and Time
- **Period**: Spring through late August of first year; Christmas/New Year period; nearly three weeks into new year (1832) just after Lords threw out Reform Bill; summer and autumn of first year; winter of first year; Vauxhall evening during spring of first year; spring of second year; **summer of second year (current narrative point)**; narrative extends into future years; present day with Fred and Mary at Stone Court in white-haired placidity
- **Primary Locations**: Middlemarch, Lowick, Grange, Freshitt, Mirecombe, Salwick, Quenwick, Fenmere, Bryngate, Chalky Flats, Gulton, Highbury, Cheltenham, Tipton, Yoddrell's farm, Frick, Miremere, Riverston, Quallingham, Halsell Wood, Loamford, Brassing, Stone Court, Coldcombe, St. Peter's Place, Lowick Gate, Shrubs, Dunholt, Yorkshire, Staveton, Bilkley, Harrowgate, Melspring, Wilhaven, Salford, Chiswick Mall, Hammersmith, Soho, Thames, England, Oxford, Chiswick Church, Buxton, Kensington turnpike, Russell Square, London, Southampton Row, Vauxhall, Exeter 'Change, India (Boggley Wollah, Ramgunge, Budgebudge, Calcutta, Dumdum), Forty Thieves theatre, King's 14th regiment post, Highbury Barn, Covent Garden Market, Doctor Swishtail's Seminary, Bedford tavern, Thames Street (City), Royal Gardens, Quenwick, Wilhaven, St. George's Hanover Square, Lambeth Palace, Cheltenham, Great Gaunt Street, Queen's Crawley (Hants), Mudbury, Gaunt Square, Mansion House, Oxford Street, Swallow Street, Cambridge, Leakington, Squashmore, Bethesda Chapel Liverpool, Naples, Paris, **Eton, Pumpernickel, Strasburg, Crawley parish**

## Main Characters

**Dorothea and Will Ladislaw (Married)**
- Engaged after Will's return; now married with infant son; established pattern of two yearly visits to Grange; Dorothea's life mixed result of young, noble impulse; finely touched spirit with fine issues though not widely visible; full nature spent in channels with no great name; effect incalculably diffusive

**Mary Garth and Fred Garth (Married)**
- Inhabit Stone Court; seen in white-haired placidity at open window; solid mutual happiness; Fred becomes distinguished county farmer; produces work on "Cultivation of Green Crops and the Economy of Cattle-Feeding" winning agricultural meeting congratulations; Fred gradually saved enough to become Stone Court owner; three boys only, youngest resembles grandfather

**Rebecca Sharp (Miss Becky)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Age and Background**: Age nineteen; father was artist/drawing teacher at Miss Pinkerton's academy—clever, prone to debt and tavern, beat wife and daughter when drunk, died after third delirium tremens; mother was French opera-girl; claims descent from noble Entrechats family of Gascony; had dismal precocity of poverty
- **Appearance**: Small, slight, pale, sandy-haired with large, odd, attractive eyes; white slender fingers
- **Accomplishments**: Speaks French with purity and Parisian accent; skilled musician and linguist; clever artist; sings better than Amelia
- **Character**: Determined to make connected plans for future; never blushed since age eight when caught stealing jam; capable of calculated charm and intimacy; droll funny creature; shows great knowledge of the world in her observations; finds devotional practices ridiculous
- **Joseph Sedley Romance Campaign**: Upon learning of Joseph Sedley's wealth, determined "If Mr. Joseph Sedley is rich and unmarried, why should I not marry him?"; invited by Amelia; won over entire household through charming behavior; left alone with Joseph in drawing-room; occupied knitting green silk purse; established great confidence and intimacy; Joseph began eloquent speech "O Miss Sharp, how--" but stopped when music ended; continued presenting nosegays; Rebecca refused his request to sing citing low spirits; asked him to help finish green silk purse; Joseph seated tete-a-tete with killing expression, hands bound in green silk web; Rebecca thought "I might go farther, and fare worse"
- **At Vauxhall**: Took Jos's arm; sat by him on open carriage box; everyone expected marriage announcement; lost themselves in solitary walk among couples; at Moscow panorama, rude fellow treading on foot caused her to fall into Joseph's arms; Joseph told favorite Indian stories again (sixth time); at supper during inebriation, Jos clasped her round waist shouting "Stop, my dearest diddle-diddle-darling"; Rebecca started but could not get away hand
- **After Vauxhall - Rejection and Departure from Sedley Household**: George Osborne pushed Jos back into seat; Jos never came; household turned against Rebecca; Blenkinsop reported Rebecca reading Mrs. Sedley's letters and accessing trinket boxes; Pinner suspected Rebecca had taken Amelia's white ribbing; entire household (except Amelia) agreed Rebecca should depart speedily; accepted Amelia's generous presents with proper hesitation; received purse from Mr. Sedley; kissing his hand, asked to consider him kind protector; behavior affecting—Mr. Sedley blessed her, invited her to always come when in town
- **Journey to Queen's Crawley**: Immediately upon departure counted guineas and began planning; carriage passed through Gaunt Square into Great Gaunt Street, stopped at tall gloomy house with hatchment over middle drawing-room window; departed London by coach early morning with bandboxes; awakened at daybreak by charwoman; placed initially inside coach but at Leakington (where rain began heavily), forced to go outside as Sir Pitt is proprietor of coach and passenger wanted inside place; rode outside in rain for greater part of way; young gentleman from Cambridge College sheltered her kindly in one of his several great coats; young Cantab (called Master Jack) and guard both knew Sir Pitt well, laughed at him, called him "old screw" (stingy, avaricious); Master Jack promised to "flog 'em on to Squashmore" in revenge for Sir Pitt's slow driving with his horses; carriage and four splendid horses with armorial bearings awaited at Mudbury, four miles from Queen's Crawley; made entrance to baronet's park in state; fine avenue of mile long leading to house; woman at lodge-gate (over pillars which are serpent and dove, supporters of Crawley arms) made curtsies as she flung open old iron carved doors
- **First Evening at Queen's Crawley**: Interrupted by Sir Pitt in night-cap and dressing-gown who seized her candle, said "No candles after eleven o'clock, Miss Becky"; called her "pretty little hussy"; threatened to come for candle every night unless she's in bed at eleven; Sir Pitt and Mr. Horrocks the butler left laughing; two immense bloodhounds let loose at night, yelling and howling at moon; Sir Pitt calls dog "Gorer" (killed a man, master of bull); calls mother dog "Aroarer" (too old to bite, formerly called Flora)
- **First Dinner at Queen's Crawley**: Half hour after arrival, great dinner-bell rung; came down with two pupils (very thin insignificant little chits of ten and eight years old, named Rose and Violet); wore Amelia's dear muslin gown; to be treated as one of family except on company days when young ladies and she dine upstairs; assembled in little drawing-room where Lady Crawley sits; at dinner, Mr. Crawley haughtily corrected the name of a dish being served; Rebecca served soup on silver soup plates with mouton aux navets; ale and water brought in wine-glasses for young ladies; after dinner, jug of hot water placed before Sir Pitt with case-bottle containing rum; Rebecca and pupils served three little glasses of wine; Lady Crawley had bumper; retired to drawing-room where Lady Crawley took enormous interminable piece of knitting; young ladies played cribbage with dirty pack of cards; one candle lit in magnificent old silver candlestick; Rebecca offered choice between volume of sermons or pamphlet on corn-laws
- **Evening Activities and Duties**: Mr. Crawley had young ladies resume yesterday's discourse, each read page of long dismal sermon delivered at Bethesda Chapel, Liverpool, on behalf of mission for Chickasaw Indians; Rebecca now engaged as governess to Rose and Violet with established daily routines at Queen's Crawley
- **Saturday Morning**: At five, heard shrieking of little black pig; Rose and Violet showed Rebecca pig yesterday; also introduced to stables, kennel, gardener picking fruit for market; girls begged for hot-house grapes but gardener said Sir Pitt numbered every grape and giving any away would cost his place; girls caught colt in paddock and asked Rebecca to ride; groom came with horrid oaths and drove them away
- **Current Status (Summer of Second Year)**: Now at Queen's Crawley estate as governess; observant of family patterns; awaits what may unfold in this employment with knowledge of the world; presents accounts of Mr. Crawley's employment are not caricatures

**Miss Amelia Sedley** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- Pupil at Miss Pinkerton's; happy, handsome, seventeen years old; loves Rebecca like sister; natural infirmity of tears; match-maker at heart; too good, too kind, doesn't know world
- Bred up for purpose of marrying George Osborne; banns read in respective families for ten years; appeared to fall in love with George at single instant when he asked her for music
- Discovered million of virtues in Rebecca; warmed into most tender friendship; showed her rooms, books, piano, dresses, necklaces, braces, laces; insisted Rebecca accept white cornelian and turquoise rings, sprigged muslin, white Cashmere shawl; entirely agreed with mother's changed opinion
- Parting with Rebecca: ransacked all drawers, cupboards, reticules, gimcrack boxes to select presents; went to Papa to beg he give his promised money to Rebecca instead; wept confidentially on Blenkinsop's shoulder about household suspicions; parting theatrical scene—one person earnest, other perfect performer; after tenderest caresses and pathetic tears with smelling-bottle; vowed to love Rebecca forever; received pathetic letter from Rebecca describing her arrival at Sir Pitt's

**George Osborne** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- Sedley's godson; family friend for twenty-three years; clever artist; bred up for purpose of marrying Amelia
- At Vauxhall: Paired with Amelia; at supper in mated pair; did not like rack punch; intervened with commotion, single push sent Jos back into seat; removed ladies in safety
- Post-Vauxhall: Found Jos groaning next morning; not pleased that family member into which he was marrying should make mesalliance with little nobody—little upstart governess; pursued advantage pitilessly; thought Jos milksop; mocked Jos relentlessly about behavior and romantic declarations; inspired distrust and hatred in Rebecca; laughed at her discomfited mien; when Rebecca came downstairs, continued liveliness and banter; told Amelia she must learn her station, called her helpless creature; said Amelia too good, too kind, doesn't know world; expressed manly compunction for unnecessary unkindness; his mockery and interference effectively discouraged Jos from pursuing proposal

**William Dobbin** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- Son of merchant/grocer; father keeps shop "Figs & Rudge" on Thames Street, City; father became Alderman Dobbin, Colonel of City Light Horse, later knighted; Dobbin entered army
- School experience: Giant amongst boys at Doctor Swishtail's Seminary, mercilessly bullied; defended George Osborne by fighting Cuff; thirteen-round left-handed fight, eventually prevailed; character rose prodigiously in estimation; name "Figs" became respectable and popular
- At Vauxhall and post-Vauxhall: Asked by George to look after shawls; carried Amelia's white cashmere shawl; paid at door for whole party; found himself humming Amelia's tune she sang on stairs; realized he was forgotten, decided he would be de trop; walked away; while walking about gardens, stepped up to supper box in agitated state when commotion seemed inevitable; shouldered off crowd
- Jos's departure: Jos seized Dobbin's hand and confided secret of his loves; Dobbin shrewdly induced him to leave gardens and hastened him to Lambeth Palace; conveyed Jos into hackney-coach depositing him at lodgings; next morning found Jos groaning on sofa, good-naturedly tended patient; entreated Osborne to have mercy when he mocked Jos
- Emotional attachment: Found himself unconsciously humming Amelia's tune; emotional attachment to Amelia beginning to develop

**Joseph Sedley** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- In East India Company's Civil Service; collector of Boggley Wollah for about eight years; caught liver complaint, returned to Europe; has own lodgings, not with family
- Very stout, puffy man in buckskins and Hessian boots with immense neckcloths, red striped waistcoat, apple green coat with steel buttons; drives horses in Park, dines at fashionable taverns, frequents theatres and opera; extremely talkative in man's society
- At Vauxhall: escorted Rebecca to dinner and gardens; at supper ordered waiters with majesty, made salad, uncorked Champagne, carved chickens, ate greater part of refreshments; insisted bowl of rack punch, drank entire contents; became inebriated, talked and laughed loudly, voluntarily sang in maudlin high key, became bold as lion, clasped Rebecca round waist shouting "Stop, my dearest diddle-diddle-darling"; continued drinking, making love, singing
- Post-Vauxhall: George Osborne pushed Jos back into seat; Jos kissed hand to retreating ladies hiccupping "Bless you!"; seized Dobbin's hand weeping, confided he adored Rebecca, broke her heart, would marry her next morning; Dobbin shrewdly induced him to leave, conveyed him home; next morning Jos groaned in severe agonies; George Osborne found him groaning on sofa; Dobbin already in room tending patient; Jos's valet Mr. Brush reported Jos "uncommon wild"
- Sent letter to Amelia apologizing for Vauxhall conduct, attributing to rack punch, announcing immediate departure for Cheltenham and later Scotland for several months; thus avoided formal proposal entirely; Jos fled town, leaving Rebecca's hopes dashed
- Old Mr. Sedley feels akin to contempt for son; says Joseph vain, selfish, lazy, effeminate

**Sir Pitt Crawley, Baronet** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Background and Ancestry**: Named after the great Commoner; son of Walpole Crawley, first Baronet, of Tape and Sealing-Wax Office in reign of George II (impeached for peculation); family tree includes John Churchill Crawley, Charles Stuart Barebones Crawley, Queen Elizabeth's Crawley (forked beard, armour); rotten borough at Queen's Crawley produces "good fifteen hundred a year"; family represented in Parliament constantly
- **Marriages and Children**: First married to Griselda/Grizzel, sixth daughter of Mungo Binkie, Lord Binkie; she brought two sons—**Pitt (named after minister)** and **Rawdon Crawley (named from Prince of Wales's friend)**; many years after Grizzel's demise, Sir Pitt led Rosa (Rose), daughter of Mr. John Thomas Dawson (ironmonger of Mudbury), to altar; by Rosa he had two daughters (Rose aged ten, Violet aged eight) for whom Rebecca Sharp now engaged as governess; Sir Pitt often told Lady Crawley (Rosa) in her lifetime she was "confounded quarrelsome high-bred jade"; when she died he kept promise never to take another of her sort
- **Estate**: Owner of Queen's Crawley estate in Hants; Queen's Crawley formerly erected by Queen Elizabeth after she was delighted with Hampshire beer; also owns Great Gaunt Street mansion in London; family estate much embarrassed; income from borough of great use to house
- **Appearance**: Old, stumpy, short, vulgar, very dirty man in old clothes and shabby old gaiters; smoking horrid pipe; shining bald head, leering red face, twinkling grey eyes, mouth perpetually on grin; when in full dress took gaiters off, showed little dumpy legs in black worsted stockings
- **Character and Behavior**: Speaks with country accent; incessantly discussing himself; swears a great deal; sometimes coarsest and vulgarest Hampshire accent; pronounces avenue as "EVENUE" and nothing as "NOTHINK"; does not disguise his qualities; proprietor of coach and horses; drives very slow; stingy, avaricious (called "old screw"); never gives money to anybody; characterization as old, stumpy, vulgar, dirty, in shabby gaiters, smokes horrid pipe, cooks his own horrid supper in saucepan; always tipsy every night; believed to sit with Horrocks, the butler after dinner
- **Treatment of Rosa (Second Wife)**: Used to get drunk every night; beat his pretty Rose sometimes; left her in Hampshire when he went to London for parliamentary session, without a single friend in wide world; Rosa had given up Peter Butt (young man who kept company with her); in consequence of disappointment in love, Peter took to smuggling, poaching, and thousand other bad courses; Rosa quarrelled with all friends and intimates of her youth, who could not be received by Lady at Queen's Crawley; found no persons willing to welcome her in new rank and abode; Sir Huddleton Fuddleston had three daughters who hoped to be Lady Crawley; Sir Giles Wapshot's family insulted that Wapshot girl not preferred; remaining baronets of county indignant at Sir Pitt's misalliance; Mrs. Bute Crawley (Rector's wife) refused to visit Rosa, saying she would never give pas to tradesman's daughter; Sir Pitt did not care, saying he had his pretty Rose and what more need man require than to please himself
- **Daily Evening Pattern**: At ten, servants called Sir Pitt and household to prayers; Sir Pitt comes very much flushed and rather unsteady in gait; has jug of hot water placed before him with case-bottle containing rum
- **Lawsuits**: Involved in numerous cases—"Crawley, Bart. v. Snaffle" (plans to throw Snaffle over), "Podder and another versus Crawley, Bart.," "Overseers of Snaily parish against Crawley, Bart." (claims common land belongs to him not parish, willing to spend thousand guineas to win)
- **Estate Management**: Has Mr. Hodson, his hind from Mudbury; discusses distraining, selling up, draining and subsoiling, tenants and farming; Sam Miles caught poaching; Peter Bailey gone to workhouse; "Serve him right," said Sir Pitt; "him and his family has been cheating me on that farm these hundred and fifty years"; told Hodson he won't let any of poacher's breed get the parsonage living; has sold the presentation of the living; numbered every hot-house grape, would not allow gardener to give any away
- **Harshness with Children**: Ordered Mr. Hodson to rush upon two little boys gathering sticks in wood with his whip; roared "Pitch into 'em, Hodson, flog their little souls out, and bring 'em up to the house, the vagabonds; I'll commit 'em as sure as my name's Pitt"
- **Wife (Rosa) - Deceased**: Called by Sir Pitt "the dowager" and "Lady Crawley"; was close but valuable woman who saved him steward; had mouldy old sampler in bedroom; had two little family pictures (young lads in college gown and red soldier jacket); slept in great front bedroom of Great Gaunt Street house; now dead

**Mr. Pitt Crawley (Eldest Son)** [MAJOR CHARACTER - NEW FOCUS]
- **Background**: Named after the great Commoner/minister; son of Sir Pitt's first marriage to Griselda/Grizzel (sixth daughter of Mungo Binkie, Lord Binkie)
- **Appearance and Manner**: Pale, thin, ugly, silent; thin legs, no chest; hay-coloured whiskers and straw-coloured hair; in full dress, pompous as undertaker; very picture of sainted mother over mantelpiece—Griselda of noble house of Binkie
- **Character**: Very earnest; high-bred propriety and respectfulness; seldom spoke to his stepmother Rosa, but when he did it was with most powerful respect; never let her quit apartment without rising in stately manner to open door and making elegant bow at her egress; taught butler to say "My lady is served" and insisted on handing her ladyship in to dinner
- **School Experience**: At Eton called "Miss Crawley"; younger brother Rawdon used to lick him violently; though his parts were not brilliant, made up for lack of talent by meritorious industry; never known during eight years at school to be subject to punishment which generally thought none but cherub can escape
- **College and Career**: Career highly creditable; prepared himself for public life through patronage of grandfather Lord Binkie by studying ancient and modern orators with great assiduity and speaking unceasingly at debating societies; had fine flux of words; delivered his little voice with great pomposity and pleasure to himself; never advanced any sentiment or opinion not perfectly trite and stale, supported by Latin quotation; failed somehow despite mediocrity which ought to have insured success; did not even get prize poem, which all his friends said he was sure of; became Private Secretary to Lord Binkie; appointed Attache to Legation at Pumpernickel, which post he filled with perfect honour and brought home despatches consisting of Strasburg pie to Foreign Minister of the day
- **Diplomatic Service**: Remained ten years Attache (several years after lamented Lord Binkie's demise); finding advancement slow, gave up diplomatic service in disgust
- **Return to England and Political Activity**: Began to turn country gentleman; wrote pamphlet on Malt on returning to England (ambitious man, always liked to be before public); took strong part in Negro Emancipation question; became friend of Mr. Wilberforce's, whose politics he admired; had famous correspondence with Reverend Silas Hornblower on Ashantee Mission; in London if not for Parliament session, at least in May for religious meetings; in country a magistrate and active visitor and speaker among those destitute of religious instruction; said to be paying addresses to Lady Jane Sheepshanks, Lord Southdown's third daughter; Lady Jane's sister Lady Emily wrote sweet tracts "The Sailor's True Binnacle" and "The Applewoman of Finchley Common"
- **Religious Activities at Queen's Crawley**: Subjected servants at Queen's Crawley to devotional exercises before mentioned (brought his father Sir Pitt to join); patronized Independent meeting-house in Crawley parish, much to indignation of uncle the Rector, consequent delight of Sir Pitt, who was induced to go himself once or twice; occasioned violent sermons at Crawley parish church directed point-blank at Baronet's old Gothic pew there; honest Sir Pitt, however, did not feel force of discourses as he always took his nap during sermon-time
- **Political Ambition**: Very earnest for good of nation and Christian world that old gentleman (Sir Pitt) should yield him up his place in Parliament; Sir Pitt constantly refused to do so; both too prudent to give up fifteen hundred a year brought in by second seat (at this period filled by Mr. Quadroon, with carte blanche on Slave question); family estate much embarrassed and income drawn from borough of great use to house of Queen's Crawley

**Lady Crawley (Rosa/Second Wife)**
- Daughter of Mr. John Thomas Dawson, ironmonger of Mudbury
- Gave up Peter Butt, young man who kept company with her; he took to smuggling, poaching, and thousand other bad courses in consequence of disappointment in love
- Quarrelled with all friends and intimates of her youth as duty bound; none could be received by her at Queen's Crawley; found no persons willing to welcome her in new rank; Sir Huddleston Fuddleston had three daughters who hoped to be Lady Crawley; Sir Giles Wapshot's family insulted; remaining baronets indignant at Sir Pitt's misalliance; Mrs. Bute Crawley (Rector's wife) refused to visit her
- Sir Pitt beat her sometimes; left her in Hampshire when went to London for parliamentary session without single friend in wide world; had mouldy old sampler in bedroom; had two little family pictures (young lads in college gown and red soldier jacket); slept in great front bedroom of Great Gaunt Street house
- **Status**: Now deceased; called by Sir Pitt "the dowager" and "Lady Crawley"; was close but valuable woman who saved him steward
- **Children**: Two daughters Rose (ten) and Violet (eight); languid dulness of their mamma did not awaken much affection in little daughters, but they were very happy in servants' hall and in stables; Scotch gardener having luckily good wife and some good children, they got little wholesome society and instruction in his lodge, which was only education bestowed upon them until Rebecca Sharp came

**Other Minor Characters**
- **Mr. Horrocks** (Butler at Queen's Crawley): Serves at meals; Sir Pitt believed to sit with after dinner; laughed with Sir Pitt when he seized Rebecca's candle
- **Mr. Hodson** (Hind from Mudbury): Sir Pitt's estate manager; discusses farming matters; jumped out of carriage at Sir Pitt's order to rush upon little boys gathering sticks; cracked whip on their shoulders at Sir Pitt's command
- **Rawdon Crawley**: Sir Pitt's younger son from first marriage; at Eton used to lick his brother Pitt violently
- **Mrs. Bute Crawley**: Rector's wife; refused to visit Rosa (Lady Crawley), saying she would never give pas to tradesman's daughter
- **Lord Binkie**: Grandfather of Mr. Pitt Crawley; patron who introduced him to public life; now deceased (lamented Lord Binkie's demise)
- **Lady Jane Sheepshanks**: Lord Southdown's third daughter; Mr. Pitt Crawley said to be paying his addresses to her
- **Lady Emily**: Sister of Lady Jane; wrote sweet tracts "The Sailor's True Binnacle" and "The Applewoman of Finchley Common"
- **Mr. Wilberforce**: Political figure whose politics Mr. Pitt Crawley admires
- **Reverend Silas Hornblower**: Had famous correspondence with Mr. Pitt Crawley on Ashantee Mission
- **Mr. Quadroon**: Currently fills second parliamentary seat for Queen's Crawley borough with carte blanche on Slave question

## Critical Facts and Status
- Narrator reflects on Vanity Fair as "a very vain, wicked, foolish place, full of all sorts of humbugs and falsenesses and pretensions"
- Narrator warns of "harrowing villainy and complicated crime" to come in story; present chapter mild compared to future chapters
- Narrator identifies self as humble servant wearing long-eared livery like congregation; promises to speak truth and reserve disagreeable strong language for mighty occasions rather than tempests in slop-basins
- Narrator states position: will introduce characters, occasionally step down from platform to talk about them; if good and kindly, love them and shake by hand; if silly, laugh at them confidentially in reader's sleeve; if wicked and heartless, abuse them in strongest terms which politeness admits
- Rebecca Sharp's accounts of Mr. Pitt Crawley's employment at Queen's Crawley are not caricatures; his devotional exercises with servants are genuine; he brought his father Sir Pitt to join them
- Parliamentary seat at Queen's Crawley worth fifteen hundred a year; family estate much embarrassed; income from borough of great use to house
- Queen's Crawley estate was formerly erected by Queen Elizabeth after she was delighted with Hampshire beer
